title: Thinking and rethinking data AI readiness - Nature Machine Intelligence
text:
Download PDF

Training machine learning models on high-quality biological datasets can quickly produce abundant results. But as datasets often evolve over time, further work is required to update models and maintain alignment between models and datasets.

Artificial intelligence (AI) applications in biological sciences thrive on high-quality datasets, and on sustained community efforts in collecting, curating, annotating, formatting and other data management tasks. The FAIR guidelines were developed to encourage good practices in ensuring that datasets are open, findable, interoperable and reusable (M. Wilkinson Sci. Data 3, 160018; 2016). However, with the fast development of AI tools, FAIR alone is no longer sufficient, and in recent years there has been a strong focus on the ‘AI readiness’ of datasets, which requires going beyond the FAIR principles. For example, Bridge2AI was launched by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in 2022 with a focus on preparing biomedical datasets for the widespread adoption of AI tools. The Open Data Institute, a UK-based non-profit organization, recently published a framework that outlines requirements for dataset AI readiness in four categories: dataset properties, metadata, surrounding infrastructure and governance. Furthermore, ‘AI-ready’ extensions to FAIR have been proposed, such as FAIR-R, which focuses on whether annotations, provenance, responsible use and documentation are sufficiently developed for machine learning.Existing efforts primarily describe the characteristics of AI-ready datasets but it is an underexplored question how AI-readiness should be sustained as biological knowledge changes over time. In a Comment in this issue, Amarda Shehu and Ruth Nussinov highlight this challenge. They point out that AI readiness cannot be an intrinsic property of biological datasets, as datasets are continuously evolving in response to discoveries, updated classifications, new acquisition strategies with higher capacity, and changes in clinical practice. Even when machine learning models are technically sound, their predictions can become misaligned with domain knowledge when shifts in input data distribution or underlying assumptions occur. The authors therefore argue that what matters is the alignment between data, models and the evolving scientific record. They focus on four questions to ask about AI-readiness: what is the intended outcome, under what assumptions, for how long, and with what safeguards. The value of these questions is that they recognize longevity as an active property of a dataset and stress the need to outline use cases, timeframes and limitations.As an example of the potential consequences of an evolving dataset, the authors highlight that between 2015 and 2023, 4.6% of 2 million clinical genetic variants were reclassified in the widely used ClinVar dataset. The dataset consists of human genetic variations and their relationships to phenotypes, which can identify diseases or at least be indicative of risk. As a result, clinical prediction models trained, for instance, on the 2022 version of the dataset can mischaracterize queried new data from 2026, potentially leading to misdiagnoses.Similar challenges arise in datasets that are intentionally designed to evolve. For example, the Gene Ontology (GO) database is dynamic, providing a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of scientific understanding of the role of genes in biology, health and disease. The GO consortium explicitly describes its annotations as a “living document” that reflects current biological understanding. But this also means that machine learning model predictions will by design diverge from domain knowledge over time as our scientific understanding advances.Keeping models aligned with evolving datasets is likely more challenging than training them in the first place. Enabling neural networks to incrementally learn from streams of data has long been recognized as an important problem in the field of machine learning, and several methods for ‘continual learning’ of models have been proposed. However, keeping models aligned with datasets also requires infrastructure that enables AI systems to detect and interpret changes in datasets. Shehu and Nussinov argue that functionality needs to be in place to better connect dataset updates to AI model developments. In particular, machine readability is essential for ensuring the long-term usability of datasets. Moreover, deployed models must be able to query dataset semantics directly, detect changes in annotations, classifications and other conceptual groupings, and adapt accordingly rather than relying on outdated assumptions.In the future, the AI readiness of datasets, and the ability of AI models to interact with them, is likely to take on a new urgency given the fast pace of AI development in scientific research. This is especially true in biological applications of AI, in which accurate predictions require datasets that are both large enough to capture variation and managed enough to preserve biological impact. AI readiness of datasets is of growing importance for scientific research, and we anticipate an important role for the specific questions asked by Shehu and Nussinov about the intended outcome, under what assumptions, for how long, and with what safeguards does AI readiness hold.
